claim: Check the Amazon page-one price spread: a tight band like $7 to $13 signals a price war; a $20 to $100 spread means buyers judge on more than price.
body: Search the product's main keyword on Amazon and note every price on page one. When near-identical items cluster in a narrow band, buyers see them as interchangeable and choose on price and review count; any new entrant has to undercut, and margins fall. The example given is tongue scrapers, where page one ran from about $7 to $13, a spread of about $6 that the seller calls a reason to walk away. When the same kind of product sells at $20, $30, $50 and $100 on one page, buyers are paying for differences in design, quality, bundle or brand, which leaves room for a better product at a higher price. How to apply: for each shortlisted candidate, record the lowest and highest price on page one for its main keyword and two or three variant keywords; drop candidates where the top price is less than about double the bottom price, then look at what the top-priced listings do differently and whether you can match it. Use this alongside the price floor and margin floor checks, not in place of them.
conditions: Private-label product selection on Amazon US; comparing listings that serve the same need.
fails_when: The wide spread comes from different products sharing one keyword (pack sizes, unrelated items), not from differentiation; the high-priced listings are established brands you cannot match.
numbers: tight band example: $7 to $13 on page one (about $6 spread) means discard
healthy spread example: $20 to $100 for near-identical products

claim: Look for Amazon products rated 4.1 to 4.3 stars that still make over $5,000 a month, and turn their 1-star complaints into the improvement spec for your supplier.
body: A product with middling ratings that still sells well proves the demand is there and that buyers are not fully satisfied. That gap is the cheapest kind of differentiation: fix what the reviews complain about. In the demo, sorting the shortlist from lowest to highest rating surfaced a patio sun shade at about $5,000 a month with roughly 300 reviews, weak photo-edited images, and 12% of reviews at one star. The seller's next step is to read those 1-star reviews, list the failures (size, colour range, durability, missing parts), and take that list to manufacturers before ordering, so the first batch already solves them. The improvement then goes into the title, bullets and images so shoppers see it. How to apply: sort research results by rating, keep products between 4.1 and 4.3 stars with at least $5,000 in monthly revenue, read every 1- and 2-star review for the top listings, group the complaints, and only proceed if a manufacturer can fix the top two or three at a cost your margin allows.
conditions: Private-label sourcing where the product can be modified at the factory; Amazon US listings with enough reviews to show patterns.
fails_when: The complaints come from shipping damage or wrong expectations rather than the product; the fix costs more than the margin allows; the low rating reflects one bad seller rather than the product type.
numbers: rating band 4.1 to 4.3 stars
at least $5,000 monthly revenue
example: 12% of reviews at one star on a roughly $5,000 a month listing with about 300 reviews

claim: Prefer Amazon products shoppers describe in dozens of ways (slim, waterproof, wallet, for men); one- or two-keyword products leave no cheap long-tail terms to launch on.
body: Amazon search works like a search engine: shoppers type many different descriptions for the same item. A phone case can be searched as slim, waterproof, wallet, green, for men, for women and so on, each a separate search with its own competition. A new listing cannot win the main term early, but it can rank on page one for many smaller descriptive terms, and those cheaper, less contested keywords are what the launch ad campaigns target first. Their combined sales build the velocity that later lifts rank on the main term. Products that are only ever searched with one or two words offer no such side doors: every sale has to come from the most competitive term, at the highest click cost. How to apply: for each candidate, pull the keyword list from a research tool and count distinct descriptive variants with meaningful search volume; favour products with dozens of them; build the launch Sponsored Products campaigns around the long-tail set and track organic rank on each.
conditions: New private-label listings on Amazon US that rely on PPC plus organic rank to build sales.
fails_when: The long-tail terms have negligible volume; the product is bought mainly through brand search or outside traffic; variants require different products (sizes, models) you do not carry.
numbers: target products with 10 to 100 descriptive keyword variants (dozens)
avoid products described by only 1 or 2 search terms

claim: Screen out Amazon private-label products under about $25: at an $8 price and $1 per click, two or three clicks per sale erase the profit.
body: On Amazon a new private-label listing pays for most early sales through Sponsored Products clicks, and click cost does not shrink with the product's price. If a click costs about $1 and an $8 item needs two or three clicks to sell once, advertising alone eats the margin before fees and product cost. Cheap products carry two more problems: a low barrier to entry (200 units at $0.75 to $2 each costs a few hundred dollars), which invites price wars, and flimsy quality, which brings bad reviews that sink the listing. The seller in this source, running two US accounts with about $102,000 in sales over 30 days, says his most profitable items all sell above $30, and screens candidates at $25 to $60. He pairs the price floor with a margin floor: at least 30% net margin after landed cost (product, freight, duties, taxes and fees to get stock into Amazon) and FBA fees. How to apply: set the research tool's price filter to $25 to $60; for each candidate estimate clicks per sale (1 divided by conversion rate) times expected cost per click, and check what is left after landed cost and FBA fees; drop anything below 30%.
conditions: US Amazon private-label launches that depend on Sponsored Products to get first sales; 2023-era click costs around $1.
fails_when: The product sells mostly through organic rank or an outside audience, so little paid traffic is needed; consumables with high repeat purchase that recover acquisition cost later; categories where click costs are far below $1.
numbers: price floor about $25, screen at $25 to $60
most profitable items above $30
$8 price at $1 per click: 2 to 3 clicks erase profit
net margin at least 30% after landed cost and FBA fees

claim: Target Amazon products whose current sellers make $5,000 to $20,000 a month; a $30,000-a-month product needs about three months of stock plus heavy launch ad spend.
body: Monthly revenue of the products you would compete with is both a demand signal and a capital requirement. Below about $5,000 a month the demand may not be worth the effort, although the seller notes products at $1,500 to $3,000 can still work. Above about $20,000, matching the leaders means funding roughly three months of inventory up front plus the advertising needed to reach that sales rate, which new sellers usually cannot afford. So the revenue filter is a budget decision, not just a demand one. How to apply: estimate the units a month you aim to sell at the target revenue, multiply by landed cost per unit and by three months of cover, then add the launch ad budget; if that total is beyond your cash, lower the revenue band until it fits. In the research tool set monthly revenue to $5,000 minimum and $20,000 maximum as a starting point, and raise the ceiling only as your inventory budget grows.
conditions: First or early private-label products on Amazon US with limited cash for inventory; FBA, where stock must be sent in ahead of sales.
fails_when: The seller has substantial capital or financing, so larger markets are reachable; fast-turning products where restock lead time is short and less cover is needed.

about 3 months of inventory needed to match a $30,000 a month product

claim: To find beatable Amazon competitors, filter for at most 300 reviews, listings at least 8 months old, at most 4 images and ungated categories.
body: Each filter removes one kind of bad candidate. A cap of 300 reviews removes listings that already have thousands of reviews, which a new listing cannot catch up with. A minimum listing age of 8 months removes fads and seasonal spikes, because the product has history across several months of demand. A cap of 4 images flags sellers who are not trying hard on the listing, which is an easy gap for a better-presented competitor. Ungated, low-risk categories (home and kitchen, patio and garden, office, pet supplies, sports and outdoors, tools) avoid products Amazon restricts or that carry patent problems; the seller lists baby, music media and battery electronics as categories that cause trouble. In one demo run these filters with a $25 to $60 price and $5,000 to $20,000 monthly revenue returned over 500 products to review. How to apply: set these filters in a product research database, vary the category so you do not end up with the same shortlist as everyone else using the same video, then apply the price-spread and review-gap checks to each result.
conditions: Private-label product research on Amazon US with a product database tool such as Helium 10 Black Box; 2023 filter set.
fails_when: Everyone copies the same filters and categories, so the shortlist is crowded; the few-images signal is out of date once most sellers use full image sets; ungated lists change by account and over time.
numbers: review count maximum 300
listing age minimum 8 months
image count maximum 4

claim: Salt & Stone earned Amazon's #1 best seller badge in deodorant before advertising there, because shoppers discovered it elsewhere and bought on Amazon for fast delivery.
body: The founder says the brand had the number one best seller badge in deodorant on Amazon before spending anything on Amazon ads, with a reported 6.3% share of the category. His explanation is cross-channel demand: people find the brand through Sephora, Erewhon, social ads or word of mouth, then check whether Amazon can deliver tomorrow or the same day, and buy there. Only later did the company actively advertise on Amazon, after which it became a major channel. He keeps the same price on Amazon as at Sephora and positions the product as an 'everybody brand' rather than a Sephora brand, which also reaches male buyers who rarely shop at Sephora. Lessons for a DTC-first brand: 1) assume off-Amazon marketing creates on-Amazon branded searches, so list and control your own listing early rather than leaving it to resellers; 2) hold price parity with key retailers to protect those relationships; 3) watch branded search volume on Amazon as a signal before investing in ads. One brand's account; the badge depends on category velocity.
conditions: DTC-first consumer brands with retail or social demand in replenishable categories where Amazon delivery speed matters.
fails_when: Brands with little off-Amazon awareness; categories dominated by private label on price; brands that cannot hold price parity across retailers.
numbers: 6.3% share of Amazon deodorant category (as stated)

claim: Since 21 January 2025 Amazon titles in most categories may not exceed 200 characters with spaces, may not use ! $ ? _ { } ^ ¬ ¦ unless part of the brand.
body: Since 21 January 2025 Amazon titles in most categories may not exceed 200 characters with spaces, may not use ! $ ? _ { } ^ ¬ ¦ unless part of the brand, and may not repeat a word more than twice. In an official Seller Forums announcement, Amazon set new product title requirements from 21 January 2025. For most product categories titles may not exceed 200 characters including spaces; some categories set a lower limit. The special characters ! $ ? _ { } ^ ¬ and ¦ are not allowed unless they are part of the brand name. A title may not contain the same word more than twice, with prepositions, articles and conjunctions exempt. Sellers can find and fix non-compliant titles in Manage All Inventory; brand owners receive suggested rewrites and have 14 days to act before Amazon updates the title itself. How to apply: write the title from the product's real attributes once, count characters with spaces, scan for the banned characters and for any word used three times (keyword stuffing usually trips this), and check the category style guide in Seller Central, which can be stricter.
conditions: Amazon listings in categories covered by the general title policy; check the marketplace's own Seller Central help for local variants such as Amazon.in.
fails_when: Categories with their own shorter limit or style guide; brand names that legitimately contain a restricted character.

claim: Amazon US charges 0.99 dollars per item (Individual) or 39.99 dollars a month (Professional) plus a referral fee that is the greater of a category percentage, often 8 to 15%, or a minimum, usually 0.30 dollars.
body: Amazon US charges 0.99 dollars per item (Individual) or 39.99 dollars a month (Professional) plus a referral fee that is the greater of a category percentage, often 8 to 15%, or a minimum, usually 0.30 dollars, on the total price including shipping. Amazon's US pricing page lists two plans: Individual at 0.99 dollars per item sold and Professional at 39.99 dollars per month. Every sale also pays a referral fee: a category percentage of the total price or a per-item minimum, whichever is greater. Most categories have a 0.30 dollar minimum. Rates range from 3% to 45% by category; examples on the page include 8% for computers and 15% for home and kitchen, toys and games, and everything else, and clothing uses tiered rates of 5%, 10% or 17% by price. The total price includes the item price, shipping and gift wrap charges, so free-shipping maths must include it. Media items add a 1.80 dollar closing fee. Fulfilment by Amazon fees are separate and estimated with Amazon's revenue calculator. How to use it: model marketplace gross profit per order with the referral fee on the shipped price plus fulfilment, storage and returns, never the referral fee alone.
conditions: Amazon.com (US) as published on the date fetched; other Amazon marketplaces such as Amazon.in have their own fee schedules.
fails_when: The seller is on another Amazon marketplace, fees have changed, or category-specific tiers apply.

claim: Amazon Vine takes products with fewer than 30 reviews, sold through FBA and, if branded, enrolled in Brand Registry; up to 30 units per product, with a fee by units charged only after a first review.
body: Amazon's Vine page sets eligibility: the product has fewer than 30 reviews on its detail page, FBA is the fulfilment method, and a branded product's brand is enrolled in Brand Registry (generic products can also qualify). Adult, digital and bundled products are not eligible. The seller can offer up to 30 units per product. The fee is per parent product: 0 for up to 2 units, 75 US dollars for 3 to 10 units and 200 US dollars for 11 to 30 units, with no extra cost for child products. Amazon charges 30 days after enrolment and after the first review is published, and charges nothing if no review arrives within 90 days. Vine Voices receive the product free and are asked for honest, unbiased opinions; the seller does not choose them or the rating. How to apply: enrol only when the product, listing and stock are final, because the 30 units go to experienced reviewers who will report every flaw; count the units as a launch cost at landed cost plus FBA fees.
conditions: Amazon.com sellers with eligible FBA products; fees are US figures on the day fetched, other marketplaces set their own.
fails_when: The product is adult, digital or a bundle, already has 30 or more reviews, or ships seller-fulfilled; fees changed after the fetch date.

up to 30 units

claim: Amazon Brand Registry needs a pending or registered trademark from an office in a country with an Amazon store, owned by the applicant, plus the brand name or logo permanently on the product or packaging.
body: Amazon's Brand Registry page lists the requirements: a pending or registered trademark for the brand name or logo, issued by a government trademark office in a country that has an Amazon store; the applicant must be the trademark owner; the mark must be a word mark or a design mark containing words, letters or numbers; and a logo including the brand name must be permanently affixed to the products or packaging. Enrolment asks for the registration or application number and the product categories. One country's office is chosen at enrolment and others can be added after approval. Registered brands get A+ Content, a free Brand Store, Sponsored Brands, Brand Analytics, Vine access and protection tools (Report a Violation, automated protections, Transparency serial codes and Project Zero for eligible brands). Brands without a trademark can use Amazon's IP Accelerator list of vetted law firms. How to apply: file the trademark first, in the exact spelling printed on the product, then enrol with the application number rather than waiting for registration.
conditions: Brand owners selling their own brand on any Amazon store; incentive amounts on the page change and are not part of this card.
fails_when: The seller is a reseller or distributor, not the trademark owner; the mark is a pure image with no letters; the brand on the product differs from the filed mark.

claim: Amazon picks the Featured Offer on total item plus shipping price, delivery speed, free shipping, free returns, seller performance and stock; reviews, star rating, Prime badge and fulfilment method are not factors.
body: In a Seller Forums announcement, an Amazon staff account said that from July 2026 Amazon is removing the separate seller eligibility requirement for the Featured Offer, rolling out across all stores by the end of 2026, while the selection method is unchanged. Offers are ranked on the combined item and shipping cost, delivery speed, free shipping, free returns, seller performance (including order volume, chargebacks and Voice of the Customer complaints) and stock availability. The post says reviews, star ratings, the Prime badge and the fulfilment method are not selection factors, and that being considered does not guarantee being featured. Amazon's suggested checks: Pricing Health for prices that make an offer ineligible, Automate Pricing rules, Voice of the Customer complaints, shipping settings, and Featured Offer percentage in Business Reports. How to apply: diagnose a lost Featured Offer factor by factor in that order before cutting price, and never match a price below the profit floor.

claim: For seller-fulfilled Amazon orders, keep late shipment rate under 4% (10 or 30 days), pre-fulfillment cancel rate under 2.5% (7 days) and valid tracking rate over 95% (30 days, per category).
body: In its Account Health Dashboard series, an Amazon staff account set the shipping performance targets for orders the seller ships. Late shipment rate is measured over 10 or 30 days and should stay under 4%; above it, the account can be deactivated. Pre-fulfillment cancellation rate is measured over 7 days and should stay under 2.5%, with deactivation possible above it. Valid tracking rate is measured over 30 days, per product category, and should stay above 95%; below it, Amazon may restrict selling non-FBA items in that category. FBA orders do not count toward these three. How to apply: when any metric nears its line, move the affected SKUs to FBA or cut the handling-time promise before fixing the process, because the short windows recover only as new clean orders replace the bad ones.
conditions: Seller-fulfilled (FBM) orders on Amazon; targets as stated by Amazon staff, checked against the live Account Health dashboard.
fails_when: All orders are FBA; the dashboard shows a different target for the marketplace or category.

claim: Amazon tells sellers to keep order defect rate under 1% and warns that breaking selling policies can cost deactivation, Featured Offer eligibility and withheld funds.
body: Amazon's Selling Partner Blog summary of seller policies says to keep the order defect rate (orders with negative feedback, an A-to-z Guarantee claim or a chargeback) under 1% to avoid restrictions on selling privileges, the late shipment rate ideally under 4% for seller-fulfilled offers, and the cancellation rate under 2.5%. claim: Amazon's search terms field has a 249-byte limit; going over can make Amazon ignore the whole field, and brand names, temporary words and subjective words are not allowed in it.
body: An Amazon staff post on listing search results reminded sellers of the 249-byte limit for the search terms (generic keyword) attribute and warned that exceeding it can cause Amazon to ignore the attribute completely. It told sellers not to enter prohibited words, giving three groups: brand names (other brands, including Amazon), temporary words such as available now, brand new, current, discounted or just launched, and subjective words such as amazing, best, cheap, effective or fastest. The limit is in bytes, not characters, so letters with accents and non-Latin scripts use more than one byte each. How to apply: fill the field with buyer words not already in the title and bullets, separated by single spaces, count bytes with a byte counter rather than a character counter, and stop at or under 249.
conditions: Amazon listings where the seller controls the search terms attribute; marketplaces may set their own limit, so check the Keyword attributes help page in Seller Central.
fails_when: A category or marketplace sets a different limit; Amazon updates the attribute rules.

claim: Basic A+ Content needs a Professional plan and Brand Registry, allows up to 5 modules (Premium up to 7), and may not contain best-selling claims, prices, shipping, warranty text, links, QR codes, contact details or competitor comparisons.
body: Amazon's A+ Content guide says Basic A+ Content is open to Professional sellers enrolled in Brand Registry, with up to five modules per ASIN; Premium A+ is for registered brands meeting further criteria and allows up to seven. Images should be no larger than 2 MB and follow the module dimensions; avoid low-resolution or animated images. Not allowed: claims such as best-selling or top-rated in text or images, warranty or guarantee information in text placements, pricing, promotional or shipping details, QR codes, hyperlinks, directions to other web pages, contact information, and any reference to or comparison with competitors. Awards must name the body and year. Content goes live after a validation step. The guide also cites Amazon internal data on sales lifts from A+; treat those as Amazon's claim, not a forecast for one product. How to apply: plan modules from buyer questions, compare only the brand's own products in comparison charts, and check every line against the banned list before submitting.
conditions: Brand-registered sellers on Amazon stores that offer A+ Content.
fails_when: The marketplace or category has its own A+ guideline; Premium criteria change.

claim: With Sponsored Products dynamic bids up and down, Amazon can raise or lower a bid by up to 100% based on likely performance, so a click can cost up to double the bid entered.
body: Amazon Ads' guide to dynamic bidding says that under dynamic bids up and down Amazon will increase or decrease bids by up to 100% for all placements based on performance, and tells advertisers to be prepared to potentially spend double the bid they input. The strategy is chosen in the campaign bidding strategy section; the alternatives are dynamic bids down only and fixed bids. The guide suggests reviewing bids about every two weeks and limiting changes while testing so results can be traced to one change. Placement adjustments for top of search and product pages stack on top of the strategy. How to apply: at launch, set the entered bid at no more than half the maximum cost per click the product can afford when using up and down, or use down only so the entered bid is the ceiling.
conditions: Sponsored Products campaigns on Amazon; check the campaign settings page for current limits, since placement caps have differed in other Amazon documentation.

claim: Amazon's allowed review routes are the Request a Review button, which sends a standard request 5 to 30 days after delivery, and Vine; incentives, review requests in packaging and asking buyers to change reviews are banned.
body: An Amazon staff post on building reviews ethically says the Request a Review button on the order details page sends a standardised review request 5 to 30 days after delivery, and that Vine is available to brand-registered sellers to jumpstart first reviews. It lists what to avoid: never offer incentives for reviews, never ask buyers to change or remove reviews, avoid messaging customers outside Amazon's system, and do not include review requests in product packaging. It recommends product quality, accurate listings, quick answers to buyer questions and easy returns. How to apply: send the button request for every eligible order rather than a chosen few, keep inserts to use and care instructions with no review request, and route complaints to support without asking for a review change.
